result:
I have a theory that most people have a private weather system. It is not metaphorical. I mean it literally. Some mornings you wake up and the air in your apartment is heavy, humid, the kind of air that makes your thoughts stick to the ceiling. Other mornings it is thin and cold and you can hear your own blood moving. I woke up this morning in a low pressure system.

The radiator was ticking. That is the sound my building makes when it is trying to be kind. It expands and contracts with a slow metallic sigh, like an old man turning over in his sleep. I lay there for a while and listened to it because the alternative was to get up and remember the entire list of things I had not done. The list was long. It always is. Pay the dentist. Call my sister back. Figure out what to do with the plant that is definitely dying but still looks hopeful.

I got up anyway. I made coffee in the chipped mug that says WORLD'S OKAYEST DAD. I am not a dad. I bought it at a thrift store because it made me laugh. It is the only mug I own that does not leak. The coffee was too hot and too bitter and perfect. I drank it standing at the kitchen window while the city assembled itself below.

I live on the fourth floor. From here the street looks like a circuit board. Cars move in red and white pulses. People walk with their heads down, phones up, and every so often someone looks up and the whole block catches their face for half a second. I watch them the way other people watch birds. I try to invent stories for them. The woman with the yellow bag is late for a job interview. The man with the dog is arguing with his mother on speakerphone. The teenager on the scooter is going to a show that will change his life.

It is a compulsion, really. I need to fill the gaps with narrative because the alternative is to accept that most lives are just a series of errands. Which is also true. Both are true at once.

There is a specific kind of loneliness that comes from being able to imagine other people's lives too vividly. You start to feel guilty for not knowing them. You start to feel lonely for them, which is a different and stranger loneliness. It is like borrowing someone else's ache and then trying to return it undamaged.

I work from home most days. I have a desk that faces a wall. I put a poster of the moon on that wall because I needed something to look at that would not ask me anything. The moon is good that way. It is always there, always changing, always indifferent. I have been staring at it for three years. Some days it is a thin line. Some days it is a bruised fullness. I have never gotten tired of it.

The work is fine. It is mostly words. I write them for other people, and then I spend my evenings trying to write words for myself that do not sound like they were written for other people. That is the hardest part. The muscle memory is too strong. You start a sentence and your brain immediately asks: Will this land? Will this be clear? Will this be liked? And then the sentence dies.

So I started doing this thing where I write for five minutes with no intention. No audience. No point. Just to see what comes out when I stop trying to be good. That is how this piece started, actually. I sat down and told myself I would write about whatever I wanted for a thousand words. No structure. No moral. Just movement.

It is funny how freeing that feels and how terrifying it is at the same time. Freedom is not the same as lightness. Freedom can be heavy. When you remove the guardrails, you realize how much you were relying on them to keep you from falling off the road. I keep typing and the radiator keeps ticking and the city keeps moving below.

I think about memory the way I think about the laundry. It piles up whether I want it to or not. I have a memory of being seven and standing in a grocery store aisle while my mother argued with a cashier about the price of oranges. I remember the smell of the oranges, the cold fluorescent light, the way my mother’s voice got higher and tighter until it almost broke. I remember thinking: I will never do that. I will never be that person. And then I was thirty and I was that person, in a different aisle, with a different kind of frustration, but the same tightness in my throat. Memory is not a lesson. It is a loop.

I also have a memory of my grandfather teaching me how to whistle by putting my fingers in my mouth in a way that made me gag. He laughed for ten minutes. I still cannot whistle. But I remember his laugh. That is the part I keep. We keep the parts that make us feel less alone.

At some point the coffee got cold. I drank it anyway. Cold coffee tastes like regret and metal. I looked at the moon poster. It was the same moon as yesterday, just a little different. I thought about how we use the word forever as if it is a solid thing. It isn’t. It is just a long series of now’s stitched together with habit.

I went for a walk at lunch. The air was that low pressure kind again. My jacket was too thin. I walked past the park where the same old man feeds the pigeons every day with a paper bag full of breadcrumbs. He nodded at me. I nodded back. We have a relationship built entirely on nodding. It is enough.

The pigeons are loud. They are not beautiful. They are not graceful. But they persist. They survive everything we throw at them. There is a kind of dignity in persistence that I admire.

I bought a peach from a cart on the corner. It was too ripe. The skin gave under my thumb like a bruise. I ate it on the bench while the wind moved through the trees and made them sound like they were whispering. I thought about how much of my life is spent waiting for something to ripen. A friendship. A project. A sense of knowing what I am doing. And how much of it is spent realizing it already is ripe and I just haven’t been paying attention.

When I got back, I found an email from my sister. She said she was sorry she hadn’t called. She said she was going through a hard time. She said she loved me. I read it three times. Then I wrote back something short and warm and then I put my phone face down and stared at the ceiling for a while. That is the whole of communication most days. A little tenderness and a lot of space.

The afternoon blurred. I answered emails. I moved numbers around in a spreadsheet. I looked up. The light had changed. The sun was lower and it came in through the blinds in stripes. I sat in one of those stripes for a minute because it felt like being chosen.

Evening came with the smell of someone cooking garlic downstairs. It made my stomach growl. I made pasta. Simple. Salt, olive oil, chili flakes. I ate it at the counter and watched the streetlights come on one by one. The circuit board got brighter.

I keep thinking about the word freely. What does it mean to write freely? Does it mean without constraint, or does it mean with the full weight of all your constraints finally visible? I think it is the second one. Freedom is not the absence of pressure. It is the ability to move with it.

I am tired now. The radiator has stopped ticking. The building is quiet. The moon poster is just a picture on a wall. The city is still moving down there, and tomorrow it will be the same and different. I will wake up in whatever weather system I have made for myself and I will make coffee in the chipped mug and I will listen for the first sound of the day.

That is enough. It has to be enough.
